Healthcare Analytics: Breast Cancer Classification Using Machine Learning Models

Kelly Adu - Gyamfi

2025-10-15

1 Data Description

Data Source:
The Breast Cancer dataset used in this study originates from the University of Wisconsin Hospitals, Madison, Wisconsin, USA, collected by Dr. William H. Wolberg of the Department of Surgical Oncology. The dataset was designed to assist in the diagnosis of breast cancer using cytological features obtained from fine needle aspirate (FNA) samples of breast masses. Each observation corresponds to a patient’s sample, characterized by ten cytological measurements describing cell nuclei appearance, along with a diagnostic label indicating whether the tumor is benign or malignant.

Original reference:
Wolberg, W. H., & Mangasarian, O. L. (1990). Multisurface method of pattern separation for medical diagnosis applied to breast cytology. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 87(23), 9193–9196.
https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Breast+Cancer+Wisconsin+(Original)

Data Generation/Collection:
The data were collected from the University of Wisconsin Hospitals, Madison, by Dr. William H. Wolberg. Cytological measurements were taken directly from digitized images of fine needle aspirate samples. Each feature is an integer value ranging from 1 to 10, representing the degree of cell abnormality. The dataset is widely used for supervised learning and binary classification benchmarking.

Size:

  • Sample size (Number of observations): 699 total records (after cleaning: 683)

  • Variables: 11 total (10 numerical predictors, 1 categorical target)

2 Formulating Practical and Analytical Questions

Developing predictive models for breast cancer diagnosis requires translating real-world clinical needs into structured analytical questions.
The dataset contains cytological features derived from fine needle aspirate (FNA) samples, each labeled as benign or malignant.
The goal is to use these measurable features to support early cancer detection through accurate and interpretable classification models.

2.1 Practical Questions

  1. Can cytological characteristics of breast cell nuclei reliably predict whether a tumor is benign or malignant?
  2. Which features contribute most to distinguishing malignant from benign tumors?
  3. Which modeling approach (logistic regression, neural network, decision tree, or ensemble) yields the most accurate and interpretable results?
  4. How can model predictions be optimized to minimize misclassification, especially false negatives (malignant cases predicted as benign)?
  5. Can predictive analytics assist healthcare professionals in making early and cost-effective diagnostic decisions?

2.2 Analytical Questions

  1. Can a binary classification model accurately predict tumor type (benign vs. malignant) based on cytological features?
  2. Which predictor variables show the strongest statistical or computational influence on malignancy?
  3. How do performance metrics (ROC-AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score) differ among the candidate models?
  4. Can neural network architectures (e.g., perceptrons with different activation functions) outperform classical models like logistic regression?
  5. Can decision trees and bagging ensembles improve performance by addressing nonlinearity and reducing model variance?
  6. Which optimal threshold maximizes diagnostic effectiveness while minimizing clinical misclassification costs?

3 Methodology

3.1 Research Design and Analytical Framework

This study employs a comparative predictive modeling approach to develop and evaluate multiple machine learning algorithms for breast cancer classification. The methodology follows a systematic pipeline encompassing data preprocessing, exploratory analysis, model development, evaluation, and interpretation.

# Split data into training and testing sets
set.seed(123)
train_index <- createDataPartition(BreastCancer_clean$Class, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_data <- BreastCancer_clean[train_index, ]
test_data <- BreastCancer_clean[-train_index, ]

cat("Training set size:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
## Training set size: 479
cat("Testing set size:", nrow(test_data), "\n")
## Testing set size: 204

4 Eploratory Data Analysis

# Feature distributions
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

# Plot feature distributions
train_data_long <- train_data %>%
  pivot_longer(-Class, names_to = "Feature", values_to = "Value")

ggplot(train_data_long, aes(x = Value, fill = Class)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~Feature, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Feature Distributions by Class",
       x = "Feature Value", y = "Density")

4.1 Summary of Key Observations from Feature Distributions

The density plots reveal clear class separation patterns between benign and malignant tumors across most cytological features.

  • Strongly Discriminatory Features: Cell.size and Cell.shape show the most distinct separation, with malignant samples concentrated at higher values (7–10) and benign ones at lower values (1–4). Bare.nuclei displays a bimodal pattern among malignant cases, suggesting variability within tumor subtypes.

  • Moderately Discriminatory Features: Cl.thickness, Marg.adhesion, Normal.nucleoli, and Bl.cromatin show partial overlap but a consistent trend of higher values for malignant cases.

  • Weakly Discriminatory Features: Epith.c.size and Mitoses have the most overlap between classes, though malignant samples still lean toward higher scores.

# Correlation analysis
library(corrplot)
numeric_data <- train_data %>% select(-Class)
cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_data)

corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "color", type = "upper", 
         tl.cex = 0.8, tl.col = "black",
         title = "Feature Correlation Matrix")

4.2 Summary of Feature Correlation Patterns

The correlation matrix highlights key interrelationships among the nine cytological features used for breast cancer classification.

Strong Correlations (r > 0.8): Cell.size and Cell.shape show an exceptionally high positive correlation (r ≈ 0.9), indicating that abnormal cells tend to have both irregular sizes and shapes. Modeling Implication: This strong association may cause multicollinearity; dimensionality reduction or selecting only one of these variables may be necessary.

Moderate Correlations (r = 0.6–0.8): Cl.thickness shows moderate relationships with Cell.size, Cell.shape, and Marg.adhesion, suggesting these traits often change together in abnormal samples. Bare.nuclei and Normal.nucleoli also correlate moderately, reflecting coordinated nuclear changes typical of malignant cells.

Overall, the correlation structure supports known biological relationships while emphasizing the need to manage redundancy in predictive modeling.

5 Model Development

5.1 Logistic Regression

glm(Class ~ ., data = train_data, family = binomial)
## 
## Call:  glm(formula = Class ~ ., family = binomial, data = train_data)
## 
## Coefficients:
##     (Intercept)     Cl.thickness        Cell.size       Cell.shape  
##        -10.3570           0.5618          -0.1234           0.3896  
##   Marg.adhesion     Epith.c.size      Bare.nuclei      Bl.cromatin  
##          0.3044          -0.0658           0.3974           0.6016  
## Normal.nucleoli          Mitoses  
##          0.3427           0.4444  
## 
## Degrees of Freedom: 478 Total (i.e. Null);  469 Residual
## Null Deviance:       620.7 
## Residual Deviance: 72.1  AIC: 92.1

5.2 Fitted Logistic Regression Model

The estimated logistic regression equation for predicting the probability that a tumor is malignant is given by:

logit(P(malignant)) = −10.357 + 0.5618(Cl.thickness) − 0.1234(Cell.size) + 0.3896(Cell.shape) + 0.3044(Marg.adhesion) − 0.0658(Epith.c.size) + 0.3974(Bare.nuclei) + 0.6016(Bl.cromatin) + 0.3427(Normal.nucleoli) + 0.4444(Mitoses)

where:

P(malignant) = eη / (1 + eη),

η = −10.357 + 0.5618X1 − 0.1234X2 + ⋯ + 0.4444X9

Interpretation

  • The intercept (-10.357) represents the baseline log-odds of malignancy when all feature values are 0.

  • Positive coefficients (e.g., Cl.thickness, Bare.nuclei, Bl.cromatin, Mitoses) indicate that increasing these features raises the likelihood of malignancy.

  • Negative coefficients (e.g., Cell.size, Epith.c.size) slightly reduce the probability of malignancy, though the magnitudes are small.

  • The model achieves a Residual Deviance of 72.1 (AIC = 92.1), indicating strong model fit relative to the null deviance (620.7).

5.3 Data Preprocessing for Neural Network

6 Model 1: Basic Perceptron with Default Parameters

# Basic perceptron model
set.seed(123)
perceptron_basic <- neuralnet(
  Class_binary ~ Cl.thickness + Cell.size + Cell.shape + Marg.adhesion + 
                 Epith.c.size + Bare.nuclei + Bl.cromatin + Normal.nucleoli + Mitoses,
  data = train_data,
  hidden = 0,  # Single layer (no hidden layers)
  linear.output = FALSE,  # Use logistic activation for classification
  act.fct = "logistic"   # Sigmoid activation function
)

# Plot the perceptron architecture
plot(perceptron_basic, 
     rep = "best",
     main = "Single-Layer Perceptron Architecture")

6.1 Summary of Model 1: Basic Perceptron (Default Parameters)

The basic perceptron used nine cytological features (Cl.thickness through Mitoses) quantitative measurements from fine-needle aspirate (FNA) images to classify tumors as benign or malignant.

  • Training Error (≈ 5.07%) – The model misclassified about 5 % of training samples, suggesting roughly 95 % training accuracy.

  • Training Steps (149) – The algorithm required 149 iterations to converge, showing the data was moderately complex but learnable.

  • Interpretation – The simple perceptron provided a solid baseline, capturing key linear patterns in the data. However, since the 5 % error refers only to training performance, further evaluation on test data is needed to confirm its true predictive ability.

6.2 Summary of Model 1: Basic Perceptron (Default Parameters)

# Plot the perceptron architecture
plot(perceptron_custom, 
     rep = "best",
     main = "Single-Layer Perceptron Architecture")

6.3 Summary of Model 2: Perceptron with Custom Parameters

The custom perceptron model was trained on the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset, using the same nine cytological features (Cl.thickness through Mitoses) to predict tumor malignancy. The neural network visualization shows a single-layer perceptron with weighted inputs directly connected to the output neuron (Class_binary).

  • Architecture: A single-layer network (no hidden layers) with 9 input neurons connected to one output neuron representing the predicted class (benign = 0, malignant = 1).

  • Key Parameters and Results:

– Training Error: 5.07 % (≈ 94.93 % training accuracy)

– Steps to Converge: 149 iterations

– Activation Function: Logistic (sigmoid)

  • Notable Weights:

– Strong positive weights for Cl.thickness (≈ 4.63), Bare.nuclei (≈ 5.53), and Bl.cromatin (≈ 6.21) — indicating these features heavily increase the probability of malignancy.

– Negative weight for Epith.c.size (≈ –1.31) — suggesting higher epithelial cell size slightly reduces malignancy likelihood.

– Bias term ≈ –6.31, adjusting the model’s baseline probability.

  • Interpretation: The custom perceptron successfully converged, maintaining the same training error (≈ 5 %) as the basic model but with stronger feature weights and stable convergence. This indicates that tuning parameters such as learning rate and optimization method improved the model’s internal stability without overfitting.

7 Model Evaluation

7.1 Prediction and Performance Metrics

# Function to evaluate perceptron model
evaluate_perceptron <- function(model, test_data, threshold = 0.5) {
  # Generate predictions
  predictions <- neuralnet::compute(model, test_data[, 1:9])
  predicted_probs <- predictions$net.result[, 1]
  predicted_class <- ifelse(predicted_probs > threshold, 1, 0)
  
  # Convert to factor
  predicted_class <- factor(predicted_class, levels = c(0, 1), 
                           labels = c("benign", "malignant"))
  actual_class <- test_data$Class
  
  # Create confusion matrix
  cm <- confusionMatrix(predicted_class, actual_class, positive = "malignant")
  
  # Calculate ROC curve and AUC
  roc_obj <- roc(actual_class, predicted_probs, levels = c("benign", "malignant"))
  auc_value <- auc(roc_obj)
  
  return(list(
    confusion_matrix = cm,
    roc_curve = roc_obj,
    auc = auc_value,
    predictions = predicted_probs
  ))
}

# Evaluate both models
eval_basic <- evaluate_perceptron(perceptron_basic, test_data)
## Setting direction: controls < cases
eval_custom <- evaluate_perceptron(perceptron_custom, test_data)
## Setting direction: controls < cases

7.2 Summary: Model Evaluation & Prediction Direction

  • This session established the critical framework for evaluating the perceptron models by defining the classification rule: “controls < cases.”

  • “controls < cases”: This defines the decision threshold. It means the model is configured to classify an instance as a “case” (malignant) if its predicted output is greater than the threshold, and as a “control” (benign) if it is less.

  • Interpretation: This setting explicitly designates “controls” as the negative class (benign tumors) and “cases” as the positive class (malignant tumors).

  • Impact on Evaluation: This directive makes the model’s False Negative rate the primary concern. In medical diagnosis, missing a malignant case (a False Negative) is a far more critical error than a False Positive.

  • Outcome: The standard 5.07% error rate is revealed to be an insufficient performance measure. Proper evaluation must now focus on metrics like Sensitivity (Recall) to ensure the model effectively identifies true cancer cases, prioritizing patient safety over raw accuracy.

8 Performance Comparison

# Compile performance metrics
performance_metrics <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Basic Perceptron", "Custom Perceptron"),
  Accuracy = c(eval_basic$confusion_matrix$overall["Accuracy"],
               eval_custom$confusion_matrix$overall["Accuracy"]),
  Sensitivity = c(eval_basic$confusion_matrix$byClass["Sensitivity"],
                  eval_custom$confusion_matrix$byClass["Sensitivity"]),
  Specificity = c(eval_basic$confusion_matrix$byClass["Specificity"],
                  eval_custom$confusion_matrix$byClass["Specificity"]),
  AUC = c(eval_basic$auc, eval_custom$auc)
)

kable(performance_metrics, digits = 3, 
      caption = "Table 1: Perceptron Model Performance Comparison") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
Table 1: Perceptron Model Performance Comparison
Model Accuracy Sensitivity Specificity AUC
Basic Perceptron 0.98 0.972 0.985 0.995
Custom Perceptron 0.98 0.972 0.985 0.995

Conclusion:

The performance of the two models is statistically indistinguishable. The customizations made to the perceptron’s parameters (e.g., learning rate, number of epochs) in this instance did not lead to any measurable improvement over the model with default parameters.

This result suggests that for this specific dataset, the basic perceptron was already operating at or near its maximum potential capability, and the chosen customizations did not alter its convergence point or predictive power.

9 Visualization of Results

9.1 ROC Curves

# Plot ROC curves
plot(eval_basic$roc_curve, col = "blue", lwd = 2, main = "ROC Curves")
plot(eval_custom$roc_curve, col = "red", lwd = 2, add = TRUE)
legend("bottomright", 
       legend = c(paste("Basic Perceptron (AUC =", round(eval_basic$auc, 3), ")"),
                  paste("Custom Perceptron (AUC =", round(eval_custom$auc, 3), ")")),
       col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "gray")

9.2 Summary: ROC Curves Visualization

The ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve plot provides a visual confirmation of the exceptional and identical performance of both perceptron models.

  • Near-Perfect Performance: Both the Basic Perceptron and Custom Perceptron have an AUC (Area Under the Curve) of 0.995. This value, being extremely close to the maximum of 1.0, indicates an almost perfect ability to discriminate between benign and malignant tumors.

  • Identical Models: The two curves are plotted on top of each other, visually demonstrating that the custom parameter tuning did not result in any performance difference from the basic model for this dataset.

  • Clinical Utility: The model’s high AUC suggests it would be an excellent diagnostic aid, capable of correctly ranking a random malignant case as more likely to be malignant than a random benign case over 99.5% of the time.

  • In conclusion, the ROC curve visualization solidifies the finding that both models are top-performing and statistically indistinguishable for this specific task.

  labs(title = "Prediction Probability Distribution by Actual Class",

       y = "Density") +

10.1 Summary: Prediction Probability Distribution

This graph shows the predicted probability distribution for both the Basic and Custom Perceptron models, separated by the actual class of the tumor (benign vs. malignant).

Key Insights:

  • Excellent Class Separation: Both models show a very clear separation between the two classes.

– Benign Tumors (Left): The predictions are strongly clustered near a probability of 0.0, meaning the models are very confident when a tumor is benign.

– Malignant Tumors (Right): The predictions are strongly clustered near a probability of 1.0, meaning the models are also very confident when a tumor is malignant.

  • High Confidence & Accuracy: The tall, narrow peaks at both ends and the very low density in the middle (around 0.5) indicate that the models are rarely uncertain. This results in the high accuracy (98%) observed previously.

  • Identical Model Performance: The distributions for the Basic and Custom Perceptron overlap completely, providing further visual proof that the custom parameter tuning did not alter the model’s behavior or performance in any meaningful way.

In short: The probability distribution confirms that both models are highly effective and confident in distinguishing between benign and malignant cases, with no practical difference between them.

# Function to find optimal threshold
find_optimal_threshold <- function(predictions, actual) {
  thresholds <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.05)
  results <- data.frame()
  
  for (thresh in thresholds) {
    pred_class <- ifelse(predictions > thresh, "malignant", "benign")
    pred_class <- factor(pred_class, levels = c("benign", "malignant"))
    
    cm <- confusionMatrix(pred_class, actual, positive = "malignant")
    
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      Threshold = thresh,
      Accuracy = cm$overall["Accuracy"],
      Sensitivity = cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
      Specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
      F1 = cm$byClass["F1"]
    ))
  }
  
  return(results)
}

# Find optimal thresholds
optimal_basic <- find_optimal_threshold(eval_basic$predictions, test_data$Class)
optimal_custom <- find_optimal_threshold(eval_custom$predictions, test_data$Class)

# Plot threshold analysis (fixed)
ggplot(optimal_basic, aes(x = Threshold)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Accuracy, color = "Accuracy"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Sensitivity, color = "Sensitivity"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Specificity, color = "Specificity"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = F1, color = "F1 Score"), linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Performance Metrics vs Classification Threshold (Basic Perceptron)",
       y = "Metric Value", color = "Metric") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Accuracy" = "blue", 
                                "Sensitivity" = "red", 
                                "Specificity" = "green", 
                                "F1 Score" = "purple"))

10.2 Summary: Performance vs. Threshold (Basic Perceptron)

This graph illustrates how the choice of classification threshold impacts the Basic Perceptron’s performance, revealing a classic trade-off between sensitivity and specificity.

Key Observations:

  • Clear Trade-Off: The most significant trend is the inverse relationship between Sensitivity (Recall) and Specificity.

  • As the classification threshold increases, Sensitivity decreases and Specificity increases.

  • This is expected: a higher threshold requires more evidence to classify a case as “malignant,” catching fewer true cancers (lower sensitivity) but also reducing false alarms (higher specificity).

  • Stable Accuracy and F1-Score: Both Accuracy and the F1-Score remain consistently high (above 0.96) across all thresholds. This indicates the model’s overall performance is robust and not overly sensitive to the specific threshold chosen.

  • Clinical Implication: The default threshold of 0.5 appears to be a well-balanced choice, providing high values for all metrics simultaneously. However, if the clinical goal were to maximize cancer detection (sensitivity) even at the cost of more false positives, a lower threshold (e.g., 0.25) would be preferable.

  • In short: The model is robust, but the optimal threshold depends on the relative importance of minimizing false negatives (prioritizing sensitivity) versus minimizing false positives (prioritizing specificity).
